Forensic Nursing

Forensic nursing — definition, role of the nurse in evidence, death certification and care of the dying and the dead.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Define forensic nursing
  • Describe the roles of a forensic nurse
  • Explain death certification and medico-legal postmortem
  • Describe care of the body for postmortem

In simple words

Forensic nursing is the care of patients who are involved in violence, crime or trauma, combined with the skilled preservation of evidence for investigation. The nurse is often the first professional the victim meets.

Roles of the forensic nurse

  • Identify victims of crime and violence early
  • Provide care, comfort and safety
  • Preserve, collect and document evidence correctly
  • Give truthful documentation and testimony
  • Support recovery, counselling and legal follow-up
  • Participate in a multidisciplinary forensic team
  • Advocate for the victim’s rights and dignity

Chain of custody

Evidence is worthless if its chain is broken. Record for every item:

  1. What was collected, from where, by whom
  2. Date and time of collection
  3. Who received it, when, and where it was stored
  4. Any transfer with signatures and seals

Death certification

  • Medical certificate of cause of death — issued by a doctor for natural death; used for registration
  • Medico-legal postmortem — ordered in unnatural or suspicious death; helps in death certificate
  • The nurse never issues a death certificate, but assists in documentation

Care of the body for postmortem

  • Confirm and record death; maintain dignity and privacy
  • Do not clean or remove artefacts if medico-legal (unless required by protocol)
  • Keep tubes, catheters and dresses in place as instructed
  • Seal and label all specimens; complete forms
  • Hand over the body with documentation to the mortuary

🔴 Broken chain loses the case

If a sample is not sealed, labelled, timed and signed, the court may reject it. The nurse protects the victim by protecting the chain of custody.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Forensic nursing pairs patient care with evidence preservation.
  2. Chain of custody records who, what, when, where for each item.
  3. Treatment always precedes evidence collection.
  4. Doctor issues the medical cause of death certificate; nurses assist and document.
  5. In medico-legal deaths, the postmortem clarifies the cause.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Testify honestly in court based on records, not memory.
  2. Never alter forensic documentation.
  3. Victims need privacy, dignity and psychosocial support.
  4. Specimens require labels, seals and prompt dispatch.
  5. Forensic nurses work with police, doctors and social workers.

📌 Memory trick

Evidence: W-H-W-W — What, How, When, Where.

60-second revision

  • Forensic nursing = victim care plus evidence preservation.
  • Roles: identify, care, preserve, document, testify, advocate.
  • Chain of custody must be unbroken.
  • Death certificate issued by a doctor; nurses document and assist.
  • Care of the body for postmortem preserves all evidence.

Test yourself

The chain of custody of evidence records:

Answer: B. The chain records what was collected, by whom, when, where stored and each transfer.

Who issues the medical cause of death certificate?

Answer: B. The attending doctor issues the cause of death certificate; nurses assist in the record.

In a medico-legal case, before postmortem the body should:

Answer: B. In medico-legal deaths, all evidence and artefacts are preserved and documented before the body is handed over.

Treatment of the victim must come before evidence collection because:

Answer: B. Life-saving care always comes first; evidence is preserved while caring, without harming the patient.

In court, a forensic nurse gives evidence based on:

Answer: B. Court evidence is based on the nurse’s documented records and is honest and factual.
